notes.text: After these things — (1.) After that act of generous charity which Abram had done, in rescuing his neighbours, God made him this gracious visit. (2.) After that victory which he had obtained over four kings; lest Abram should be too much elevated with that, God comes to tell him he had better things in store for him. The word of the Lord came unto Abram - That is, God manifested himself to Abram, in a vision - Which supposeth Abram awake, and some sensible token of the presence of the divine glory, saying, Fear not Abram - Abram might fear lest the four kings he had routed, should rally and fall upon him. No, saith God, fear not: fear not their revenge, nor thy neighbour's envy; I will take care of thee. I am thy shield - Or, emphatically, I am a shield to thee, present with thee, actually defending thee. The consideration of this, that God himself is, a shield to his people, to secure them from all destructive evils, a shield ready to them, and a shield round about them, should silence all perplexing fears. And thy exceeding great reward - Not only thy rewarder, but thy reward. God himself is the felicity of holy souls; He is the portion of their inheritance, and their cup.

Behold to me thou hast given no seed — Not only no son, but no seed. If he had had a daughter, from her the promised Messias might have come, who was to be the Seed of the Woman; but he had neither son nor daughter.

And he brought him forth — It seems, early in the morning, and said, look now toward heaven, and tell the stars: so shall thy seed be -

1. So innumerable, for so the stars seem to a common eye. Abram feared he should have no child at all, but God tells him his descendents should be so many as not to be numbered.

2. So illustrious, as the stars of heaven for splendour; for to them pertained the glory, Rom. ix, 4. Abram's seed according to the flesh were like the dust of the earth, Chap. xiii, 16, but his spiritual seed are like the stars of heaven.

And he believed in the Lord — That is, believed the truth of that promise which God had now made him, resting upon the power, and faithfulness of him that made it: see how the apostle magnifies this faith of Abram, and makes it a standing example, Rom. iv, 19-21. He was not weak in faith; he staggered not at the promise: he was strong in faith; he was fully persuaded. The Lord work such a faith in every one of us. And he counted it to him for righteousness - That is, upon the score of this he was accepted of God, and, by faith he obtained witness that he was righteous, Heb. xi, 4. This is urged in the New Testament to prove, that we are justified by faith without the works of the law, Rom. iv, 3,Gal. iii, 6, for Abram was so justified, while he was yet uncircumcised. If Abram, that was so rich in good works, was not justified by them, but by his faith, much less can we. This faith, which was imputed to Abram for righteousness, had newly struggled with unbelief, ver. 2, and coming off, conqueror, it was thus crowned, thus honoured.

I am the Lord that brought thee out of Ur of the Chaldees — Out of the fire of the Chaldees, so some: that is, from their idolatries; for the Chaldeans worshipped the fire. Or, from their persecutions. The Jewish writers have a tradition, that Abram was cast into a fiery furnace for refusing to worship idols, and was miraculously delivered. It is rather a place of that name. Thence God brought him by an effectual call, brought him by a gracious violence; snatched him as a brand out of the burning. Observe how God speaks of it as that which he gloried in. I am the Lord that brought thee out - He glories in it as an act both of power and grace. To give thee this land to inherit it - Not only to possess it, but to possess it as an inheritance, which is the surest title. The providence of God hath secret, but gracious designs in all its various dispensations: we cannot conceive the projects of providence, 'till the event shews what it was driving at.

Whereby shall I know that I shall inherit it? — This did not proceed from distrust of God's power or promise, but he desired this,

1. For the strengthening of his own faith. He believed, ver. 6, but here he prays, Lord help me against my unbelief, Now, he believed, but he desired a sign, to be treasured up against an hour of temptation.

2. For the ratifying of the promise to his posterity, that they also might believe it.

Take me an heifer — Perhaps Abram expected some sign from heaven, but God gives him a sign upon a sacrifice. Those that would receive the assurances of God's favour, must attend instituted ordinances, and expect to meet with God in them. Observe,

1. God appointed that each of the beasts used for his service should be three years old, because then they were at their full growth and strength. God must be served with the best we have.

2. We do not read that God gave Abram particular directions how to manage these, knowing that he was well versed in the custom of sacrifices.

3. Abram took as God appointed him, though as yet he knew not how these things should become a sign to him. He divided the beasts in the midst, according to the ceremony used in continuing covenants, Jer. xxxiv, 18, 19, where it is said, they cut the calf in twain, and passed between the parts.

4. Abram, having prepared according to God's appointment, set himself to expect what sign God would give him by these.

And when the sun was going down — About the time of the evening oblation. Early in the morning, while the stars were yet to be seen, God had given him orders concerning the sacrifices, ver. 5, and we may suppose it was at least his morning's work to prepare them, and set them in order; which when he had done, he abode by them praying and waiting 'till towards evening. A deep sleep fell upon Abram - Not a common sleep through weariness or carelessness, but a divine extasy, that being wholly taken off from things sensible, he might be wholly taken up with the contemplation of things spiritual. The doors of the body were locked up, that the soul might be private and retired, and might act the more freely. And lo, a horror of great darkness fell upon him - This was designed to strike an awe upon the spirit of Abram, and to possess him with a holy reverence. Holy fear prepares the soul for holy joy; God humbles first, and then lifts up.

glossa.text: « These things therefore being done, » etc., « Fear not. » When the multitude of vices has been triumphed over, the hope of every faithful man is strengthened by the Lord, that it may not waver, but may look for its reward.
« And Abram said. ((HIERON. in Q. Hebr.)) « I go without children, » etc. *as far as* from him, they say, Damascus was both named and founded.

« Look up to heaven, » etc. Above he said: « Thy seed shall be as the sand of the sea, » because in that people some were carnal and earthly, who are compared to sand, since they are dry and unfruitful of good works; others were as shining stars.

((RAB.)) A twofold signification of the promised seed is given. When the stars are shown, it is said to him: « So will I make thy seed, » that is, the Christian nation, whose father thou art to be in faith, namely to glitter with the light of the resurrection. But when the sand is shown, it is said: « So shall thy seed be, » etc., that is, the nation of the Jews shall be numerous, but dry and unfruitful.

« Take me, said he, » etc. ((ISID. in Gen., tom. V.)) The heifer of three years, the Jewish people set under the yoke of the law, etc., *as far as* when by fire the good shall be separated from the evil.

« A heifer of three years, and a she-goat of three years, » etc. Because from Adam to Noah, and thence to Abram, and then to David, the people grew up.

« And the birds came down, » etc. *((GREG., lib. XVI Moral., c. 20.)) Tropologically.* In the very sacrifice of prayer importunate thoughts thrust themselves in, desiring to snatch it away or to violate it: but with the hand of holy discretion we ought to guard what we offer without, lest malignant spirits and perverse thoughts snatch it away.

« Dread rushed in, » etc. ((AUG. in Quaest. Hebr.)) This question is to be handled on account of those who contend that these disturbances do not fall upon the mind of the wise man, etc., *as far as* a disturbance not to be named.

notes.text: Light — My counsellor in all my difficulties, and my comforter and deliverer in all my distresses. Strength - The supporter and preserver of my life.
In this — That God is my light.

Dwell. &c. — Have opportunity of constant attendance upon God. To behold - That there I may delight myself, in the contemplation of thy amiable and glorious majesty, and of thy infinite wisdom, holiness, justice, truth, and mercy.
The secret — In his tabernacle, into which mine enemies cannot come. He alludes to the ancient custom of offenders, who used to flee to the tabernacle or altar. Rock - A place high and inaccessible.
Away — From thy face or presence, or from the place of thy worship.
Because of — That I may neither fall into their hands by my folly, nor give them any occasion of triumphing over me.

The living — David was thus earnestly desirous of this mercy in this life, not because he placed his portion in these things; but because the truth and glory of God, were highly concerned in making good the promise of the kingdom to him. A prayer for help, ver. 1-3. The doom of the wicked, ver. 4, 5. A thanksgiving, closed with prayer, ver. 6-9. A psalm of David.

glossa.text:
*Unto the end.* ((AUG., CASS.)) First, David chosen, etc., *as far as* whence groaning and labouring in the sacrament; that he may rejoice in the reality.

 *The Lord is my light,* etc. ((CASS.)) Of the first anointing, through which the second is made sure, he speaks here.

*The Lord is the protector of my life.* ((AUG.)) He gives the life of the virtues, which he also protects, without which all his gifts are lost.

*Of whom shall I be afraid?* ((ID.)) Whom should the flesh fear, when it shall have put on corruption *corruptionem*; read *incorruptionem*, "incorruption".

*The wicked upon me.* ((ID.)) That, insulting, they may prefer themselves to me: which God turns to the better, so that with their cursing tooth they consume not me, but my carnal desires. Or *let them eat,* that is, let the cruelty of my enemies take its delight in my death, *the flesh;* the soul they cannot.

*They were weakened.* ((ID.)) While Christ took flesh, they were made to waver, and afterwards submitted themselves wholly to faith.

 ((CASS.)) Or, being weakened little by little they came to the ruin of the soul.

*Camps.* ((CASS.)) Efforts, battle, conflicts.

*In this will I hope.* ((AUG.)) I have hope of victory in the Lord of the eternal reward.

*One thing I have asked.* ((AUG.)) This one house is eternal, in which one may abide always, where the days are eternal; why there? That I may contemplate the delight of God, which is the true good.

*All the days of my life.* ((AUG.)) That as long as I live, etc., *as far as* I will make manifest the work.

*That I may see.* ((ID.)) Another reading: *That I may contemplate the delight of the Lord,* that is, to this end, that at last he may appear, etc., *as far as* and therefore not rashly do I ask *one thing,* though a sinner.
*In secret*: ((AUG.)) as it were there are many parts, etc., *as far as* him whom presently he calls a rock.

*I have gone round.* ((AUG.)) Because he offered himself to me as a leader, etc., *as far as* that I might fulfil all his wills.

((HIER.)) Or I have looked round upon all created things, or the examples of the saints.

((AUG.)) I have gone round in mind all created things, etc., *as far as* the more ardently it desires.
*Hear, O Lord, my voice,* etc. ((CASS.)) What labour, what groaning? The prayer before the second anointing, that he may be able to have that which he also promises himself by the spirit of prophecy.
*To thee hath said.* ((CASS.)) *The heart,* the reason taught by thee, converses with thee of the one thing, that it may handle nothing other than what thou teachest.

*Turn not away.* ((AUG.)) Another asks here for temporal goods from God, and rejoices in what is given; this man asks nothing but *one thing.* Another, having them, fears him angered, lest he take them away; this man thinks there is no anger unless he *turn away his countenance,* even if he punish something in him; nothing more divine could he have said.

*Turn not aside.* ((AUG.)) He does not turn aside in anger, when he turns his face from sins; or, *turn not aside,* so as to let me slip in anger, that is, in what thou mayest punish; but that our weakness may be made more wary.

 *My saviour,* etc. ((AUG.)) As though: in vain hast thou created and re-created, etc., *as far as* he was chosen by the Lord through Samuel.

*For my father,* etc. He made himself a little one to God, and made him his own *father:* because he commands, calls, founded and rules. *A mother,* because he cherishes, contains, suckles and nourishes; but the world is a father, or the devil, the mother Babylon, that is, the fellowship of the wicked.
*Set me a law,* etc.
*Of them that trouble me.* ((CASS.)) As of Saul and his helpers, etc., *as far as* because they are false.

*I believe to see.* ((AUG.)) But among all perils, God directing, I believe to see.

*Good things.* ((ID.)) Good things which are true, eternal. Those men persuade to a blessedness in this earth, which is the earth of the dying.
*Expect.* ((CASS.)) As I am sure of it, etc., *as far as* endure what thou sufferest.

notes.text: Mark them — For your imitation.
Weeping — As he wrote. Enemies of the cross of Christ - Such are all cowardly, all shamefaced, all delicate Christians.

Whose end is destruction — This is placed in the front, that what follows may be read with the greater horror. Whose God is their belly - Whose supreme happiness lies in gratifying their sensual appetites. Who mind - Relish, desire, seek, earthly things.
Our conversation — The Greek word is of a very extenslve meaning: our citizenship, our thoughts, our affections, are already in heaven.

Who will transform our vile body — Into the most perfect state, and the most beauteous form. It will then be purer than the unspotted firmament, brighter than the lustre of the stars and, which exceeds all parallel, which comprehends all perfection, like unto his glorious body - Like that wonderfully glorious body which he wears in his heavenly kingdom, and on his triumphant throne.
So stand — As ye have done hitherto.

glossa.text: *Enemies of the cross.* They who bring in the observances of the flesh assert the cross to be superfluous.

*Whose God is their belly.* As though salvation were in food, so that the belly is a god, and they glory in the parts of shame, circumcised *circumcicis*, which is to be wise in earthly things, and whatsoever they do, they do it for the belly. Or, the foods which belong to the belly they make a god: while they say that these justify men, and their glory is in such things, whereby they may be confounded and put to the blush, while they say that they are justified through temporal things. And so their temporal glory shall lead them to eternal confusion.
*Our conversation.* That is, in living and in understanding let us be like the angels. Whence also, that is, besides the goods which we already have, *we also look for the Lord.*

*Joy, and consolation.* That is, through whom I am gladdened in the present and shall be crowned in the future. For when the disciples are victors in the contest, the master will be worthy of the crown.

notes.text: Herod is minded to kill thee — Possibly they gave him the caution out of good will.

And he said, Go and tell that fox — With great propriety so called, for his subtilty and cowardice. The meaning of our Lord's answer is, Notwithstanding all that he can do, I shall for the short time I have left, do the works of him that sent me. When that time is fulfilled, I shall be offered up. Yet not here, but in the bloody city. Behold, I cast out devils - With what majesty does he speak to his enemies! With what tenderness to his friends! The third day I am perfected - On the third day he left Galilee, and set out for Jerusalem, to die there. But let us carefully distinguish between those things wherein Christ is our pattern, and those which were peculiar to his office. His extraordinary office justified him in using that severity of language, when speaking of wicked princes, and corrupt teachers, to which we have no call; and by which we should only bring scandal on religion, and ruin on ourselves, while we irritated rather than convinced or reformed those whom we so indecently rebuked.
It cannot be, that a prophet perish out of Jerusalem — Which claims prescription for murdering the messengers of God. Such cruelty and malice cannot be found elsewhere.
How often would I have gathered thy children together — Three solemn visits he had made to Jerusalem since his baptism for this very purpose. Matt. xxiii, 37.

Your house is left to you desolate — Is now irrecoverably consigned to desolation and destruction: And verily I say to you, after a very short space, ye shall not see me till the time come, when taught by your calamities, ye shall be ready and disposed to say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord. It does not imply, that they should then see Jesus at all; but only that they would earnestly wish for the Messiah, and in their extremity be ready to entertain any who should assume that character.

glossa.text: *Say ye to the fox,* etc. The fox is a crafty animal, lurking in a hole for ambush, foul of smell, never going by straight paths. All these things suit the heretics, whose type Herod holds, who strive to quench Christ, that is, the humility of the Christian faith, in them that believe. *Behold I cast out demons,* etc. As if he said: Neither Herod nor the heretics, of whom he himself is the figure, shall be able to disturb what I purpose to do. And I purpose to cast out demons from the hearts of men, that, leaving vanities behind, they may believe in me; and to perfect healings, that they may live according to my precepts; afterwards I am consummated in my body, which is the Church, which, glorified on the day of the resurrection, I shall bring to the fellowship of the angels.

*Nevertheless I must.* Herod shall not be able to disturb it but that I so act and am so consummated; nor shall he be able to work the death of my body, which must come to pass in Jerusalem, where not he but Pilate bears rule. *To-day and to-morrow,* etc. The first day is to renounce vanities through the grace of God. The second, to be in accord with the truth in manners and in life. The third is the final glorification.

*Jerusalem,* etc. Where my prophets are, there I, the head of the prophets, must be sacrificed; for which sin she herself shall justly be destroyed, and with that destruction of theirs I grieve as a devoted father. *How often would I have gathered.* As if he said: I would, and thou wouldest not: and as many as I have gathered by my will, which is always effectual, I did it while thou wast unwilling, because thou hast always been ungrateful. *Thy children.* In this, that he says: *How often would I have gathered thy children,* etc., he bears witness to all the prophets sent by him in time past. *Even as a bird,* etc. Beautifully does he who had called Herod a fox, while he was plotting his death, compare himself to a bird, because the deceitful fox always lays ambushes for birds.

*Your house.* The temple or the city, because, the Lord being slain, the Romans, plundering as it were an empty nest, took away both the place and the nation. *You shall not see me,* etc. Unless you do penance and confess me to be the Son of the almighty Father, you shall not see my face at the second coming. *When you shall say,* etc. This indeed the crowds said when the Lord was coming into Jerusalem. But because Luke does not say that the Lord afterwards returned to the Galileans, so that this might be chanted to him by them, he compels it to be understood mystically of the coming of his brightness.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Look up — the stars are past counting, and so is the promise.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
The Lord is our light; whom shall we fear?
We wait for the Lord; we take heart.
Like a hen over her brood, God longs to gather us.
Gather us, Lord, and lead us home.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: How often the mother bird spreads her wings over the brood, calling the scattered chicks back beneath her warmth.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Count the stars, if you can — God's promise outruns the night sky, older than your fear, surer than the dark.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
The Lord is our light and our salvation; though the foxes prowl, we will not be afraid.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
So come under the shadow of those wings, and set your face with him toward the city.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.
